items.prompt: The finance ministry plans next year's public services: it expects N$64 billion of revenue and intends N$72 billion of spending on schools, clinics and roads. Define the government budget.
items.canonical_answer: The government budget is the government's yearly plan of the revenue it expects to raise, mostly from taxes, set beside the spending it intends on public services. Here N$64 billion of expected revenue against N$72 billion of spending means N$8 billion must be borrowed.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a yearly plan of expected revenue set beside intended spending, not the cash the government happens to hold.
The meaning must pair both sides of the plan - revenue and spending; a definition that names the spending while leaving the revenue out earns little.

items.prompt: Namibia's budget statement arrives each year with revenue estimates on one side and departmental spending plans on the other. Identify the features a government budget includes.
items.canonical_answer: A government budget includes expected revenue, the tax and other receipts the government forecasts; intended spending, set out department by department for schooling, health care and roads; and, where the two sides do not match, the borrowing that bridges the gap.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - expected revenue, intended spending and any borrowing that bridges the gap - as parts of the yearly plan.
What it includes must be features of the plan itself; a list of things the government happens to spend on, with no plan element around them, earns little.

items.prompt: Street lighting over Otavi's taxi rank cannot be confined to those who pay for it, so no private firm installs any. Define a public good, and state why the government funds this lighting.
items.canonical_answer: A public good is non-excludable, so non-payers cannot be kept from its benefits, and non-rival, so one person's use leaves as much for others. Because firms cannot charge every user, they tend to provide too little, so the government funds the lighting.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a public good with its two features - non-excludable and non-rival - and the under-provision that follows when the market is left alone.
The meaning must state why the market fails to fund the lighting; a definition that treats public spending as good in itself earns little.

items.prompt: The budget commits N$500 million to resurfacing the road from Outjo to the Etosha gate, with road crews in the district idle and lodges along the route paying some of the region's lowest wages. Analyse the consequences of this spending for the road crews, the lodges and the government's budget.
items.canonical_answer: When N$500 million of public spending reaches a district where road crews are idle, there is spare capacity to draw on. Because the contractors hire the crews, wages rise and circulate through the towns along the route, and the better road lowers the cost and risk of the journey, so more visitors reach the lodges. Therefore the crews gain work and wages, the lodges gain trade and their low-paid staff gain hours, and the government's budget carries the N$500 million now, financed from revenue or borrowing; any borrowing is repaid by later taxpayers.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - N$500 million committed to resurfacing - must be named first, together with the idle crews.
Mechanism: because the spending reaches workers with spare capacity, this causes incomes and then trade to rise; the wage chain must be traced.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the crews, the lodges and their workers, the budget - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the road crews, the lodge staff, the taxpayer.

items.prompt: The state clinic in Gobabis treats 4 000 patients a season free of charge, while a private pharmacy on the same street sells the same treatments to those who can pay. Explain, for this town, why the government rather than the pharmacy funds the clinic.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show 4 000 patients treated free whether or not they can pay, which a private seller would not do: treatment is a merit good that households tend to under-consume when asked to pay. Because households that cannot pay would go untreated by the pharmacy, the market alone provides less treatment than the town needs. Public provision corrects this and redistributes care towards poorer households. Therefore the government funds the clinic so that treatment depends on need rather than payment, while the pharmacy serves those who choose to pay.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: 4 000 patients treated free against the pharmacy's paying customers - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because untreated households make the under-consumption real, the link is the merit-good case for public provision.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close the loop on why the state pays and the private seller does not.

items.prompt: The ministry can either spend N$1.2 billion over three years on free textbooks and school meals for the poorest regions or use the same sum to cut taxes for small firms. Discuss whether the spending programme is the better use of the N$1.2 billion.
items.canonical_answer: On balance the spending programme is likely to be the better use, though the judgement depends on delivery and on how firms would use a tax cut. The programme could be better because textbooks and meals are merit goods that low-income households under-consume when they must pay, so public provision reaches children whose families cannot buy them; the meals also transfer spending power to the poorest households, narrowing the income gap; and the money goes straight into schools. It might not be, because small firms may use a tax cut to hire, and where there is spare capacity that raises output and jobs directly; the schemes may leak into administration; and meals from central depots may take trade from local food sellers. What settles it is delivery: whether the schemes reach the regions they target, and whether firms would hire or simply hold the money. Judged on reach to the poorest, the programme is stronger; judged on speed to jobs, the tax cut may be.
marking_guidance: The judgement must be stated and be decisive: on balance the programme or the cut, with its reason.
Why it might: the case for - merit-good provision and redistribution reaching the poorest households - developed to its consequence.
Why it might not: the case against - firms hiring where there is spare capacity, delivery leaking, trade displaced - developed to its own consequence.
The condition it depends on: what settles it is delivery against the firms' hiring response; answers that name no decisive condition stall in the middle band.

items.prompt: Every wage packet at Oshakati Textiles loses a slice to income tax before it is paid, and every lunch bought at the factory gate carries value-added tax, collected by the seller and added to the bill. Define taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Taxation is the set of compulsory payments a government levies on the incomes, spending or wealth of households and firms, collected to finance public spending; a payment is a tax where the law requires it regardless of any specific service received in return.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: compulsory payments levied on income, spending or wealth to finance public spending, not prices paid for services.
The meaning must state that the payment is compulsory whatever service is received; the case shows it on income (the wage packet) and on spending (the lunch bill).

items.prompt: The government adds N$6 to the duty on a carton of cigarettes sold at Oshakati's open market, where stalls sell 2 000 cartons a month at N$30 and the state clinic spends N$250 000 a month on the chest cases that follow. Analyse the consequences of the duty for the stallholders, the smokers and the clinic.
items.canonical_answer: The duty rise of N$6 lifts the stall price from N$30 to N$36, since 30 + 6 = 36. Because the price now carries more of the harm the clinic pays for, the quantity demanded tends to fall: some smokers buy fewer cartons, some quit, and some switch to cheaper or untaxed sources. Therefore the stallholders sell fewer cartons and their takings may fall; smokers who keep buying pay more, the heaviest hit hardest; and the clinic's case load may ease. Where habit keeps demand strong, the fall may be small and the duty works mainly as a revenue raiser for the treasury.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the duty rising by N$6, moving the carton from N$30 to N$36 - must be named first.
Mechanism: because the price carries more of the harm the clinic pays for, this causes the quantity demanded to tend to fall.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the stallholders, the smokers, the clinic - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the stallholder, the smoker, the clinic's patients.

items.prompt: A Katutura clinic spends N$400 000 a season treating the chest cases that follow smoking, and a pack of 20 already carries N$10 of duty at its N$30 price. Explain, for this neighbourhood, why the government taxes tobacco rather than banning it outright.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show N$400 000 of clinic spending a season that the N$30 price leaves out, with N$10 of duty already making the price carry part of that harm. Because a tax raises the price buyers pay, it discourages young and light smokers first while still raising revenue for the clinic. A ban would push the same buying into unrecorded channels, where there is no price signal and no revenue. Therefore the government taxes rather than bans: the duty steers buying away from tobacco and helps fund treatment.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: N$400 000 of clinic spending against the N$10 already carried by the pack - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the duty moves the price towards carrying the harm, the link is discouragement plus revenue, against a ban's uncollectable underground.
Conclusion: therefore tax rather than ban, with the reason drawn from the data.

items.prompt: Chest wards at the state hospital are full year-round, market traders fear for their trade, and the treasury proposes a further duty rise on tobacco. Discuss whether taxing tobacco more heavily is justified.
items.canonical_answer: On balance a further rise is likely to be justified on health grounds, though it depends on how strongly smokers respond to the price and where the revenue goes. In its favour, the duty makes the price carry more of the cost that fills the wards, discouraging new smokers first and pushing others to quit, and the revenue can fund the same wards. Against it, the burden is regressive, falling hardest on poor households whose smokers keep buying; where habit keeps demand strong, the quantity may barely fall, so the rise raises revenue more than it improves health; and buying may leak into untaxed informal channels, costing traders their trade while the clinic sees little relief. What settles it is how strongly the quantity demanded responds: if strongly, the duty works as a health measure; if weakly, it mainly taxes poor smokers' habit.
marking_guidance: The judgement must be stated and be decisive: on balance for or against the rise, with its reason.
Why it might: the case for - the price carrying the harm, discouragement and revenue for the wards - developed to its consequence.
Why it might not: the case against - the regressive burden, demand that barely answers the price, leakage into untaxed channels - developed to its own consequence.
The condition it depends on: what settles it is how strongly quantity demanded responds to the price; answers that name no decisive condition stall in the middle band.

items.prompt: At Marula Foods in Gobabis, the company pays tax on its profits out of its own account, while its customers pay value-added tax on every order, added to the bill and handed over by the firm. Define a direct tax and an indirect tax.
items.canonical_answer: A direct tax falls on income or profit and is paid by the taxed party itself, as with Marula Foods' profit tax. An indirect tax falls on spending and is collected from buyers by the seller, as with the value-added tax on each order.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition of each: the direct tax falls on income or profit and is paid over by the taxed party, while the indirect tax falls on spending and is collected by the seller.
The meaning must hold the boundary the case gives - who hands the charge over, and what it falls on - which is what sorts the two taxes apart.

items.prompt: In one country, a worker earning N$10 000 a month pays N$1 500 of income tax while a worker earning N$30 000 pays N$6 000, and every household, whatever it earns, pays 15 per cent value-added tax on its shopping. Identify the features that make the income tax progressive and the value-added tax regressive in its effect.
items.canonical_answer: The income tax takes 15% of the N$10 000 wage but 20% of the N$30 000 wage: a rising share, so progressive. Flat 15% value-added tax takes a larger share of a poorer household's income, since it spends more of what it earns: regressive.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - the rising share for the income tax and the larger share of a poor household's income for the value-added tax - as shares, not amounts.

What it includes: a regressive tax is classified by the share of income it takes, not by a falling rate; a value-added tax at a flat rate is regressive because the poor spend a larger part of their incomes.

items.prompt: A duty rise at Walvis Bay lifted the price of a litre of fuel, and haulage firms have since cut their routes; one firm's ledger also shows income tax paid on its profits, straight from its own account. Explain, for this port town, the classification of the two taxes and the direction in which the events ran.
items.canonical_answer: The extract shows two charges on one haulier. The fuel duty is an indirect tax: it falls on spending and is collected from buyers by the fuel station. The profit tax is direct: it falls on income and is paid by the firm from its own account. The duty rise raised fuel costs and the route cuts followed, so the cuts are a consequence of the tax increase, not its cause. Therefore the events run from the tax change to the routes.
marking_guidance: The context - the data: the duty at the pump against the profit tax paid from the firm's own account - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the sorting turns on what the charge falls on and who hands it over, the link is the direct-against-indirect boundary.
Conclusion: therefore the direction must be stated plainly - the duty rise is the cause, the route cuts are consequences of an increase in taxes, never the cause of it.

items.prompt: Namibia's income tax is deducted from wages before they are paid, its rates are published in advance, and its rules state plainly what is due from whom and when. Define the principles of certainty and convenience in taxation, using this system.
items.canonical_answer: Certainty means the payer knows what is due, when and how, as rates published in advance and plain rules show. Convenience means tax is easy to pay where and when it falls due, as deduction from wages before they are paid shows.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition of each principle: certainty, that the payer knows what is due, when and how; convenience, that payment is easy where and when it falls due.
The meaning must attach each principle to the feature of the system that shows it; a bare list with no feature attached earns little.

items.prompt: In one country the income tax rates for the year ahead are published before the year begins; in another they are announced after incomes have been earned and spent. Explain why certainty is treated as a principle of good taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Certainty matters because a payer who knows in advance what is due, when and how can plan spending, saving and work around the tax, and the government's revenue flows steadily. Where rates are announced after incomes are earned, payers cannot know what an hour of work or a season of trading will leave them, so effort and investment tend to shrink, disputes with the tax authority rise and revenue becomes unreliable. An unpredictable tax, however fair on paper, fails the payer in practice.
marking_guidance: The reason or purpose of the principle must be stated: a payer who knows what is due can plan, so the revenue flows steadily.
Why it matters must run through the contrast the prompt gives - rates known in advance against rates announced after the fact - each with its consequence.
Because the reason runs through choices, reward the link between certainty and the effort and investment households and firms make.

items.prompt: A market trader at Katima Mulilo pays a flat N$20 daily stall fee whatever her takings, while her cousin, a salaried engineer in Windhoek, has income tax deducted from a wage that rises with each promotion. Explain, from these two cases, which system better follows the equity principle and why.
items.canonical_answer: The trader pays a flat N$20 a day whatever her takings, while the engineer's tax rises with each promotion. Equity asks that those more able to pay bear a larger share. Because the fee takes the same N$20 from a thin day as from a good one, it takes a larger share of a poor trader's income, whereas the engineer's tax rises with her ability to pay. Therefore the salary-based income tax better follows equity, though the flat fee scores on economy because it is cheap to collect.
marking_guidance: The context - the data: the flat N$20 fee against the rising deduction from the engineer's wage - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because equity turns on ability to pay, the link is the share each system takes from thin earnings against rising ones.
Conclusion: therefore the salary-based system better follows equity, with the fee's economy acknowledged as the trade-off.

items.prompt: A nurse at Otjiwarongo takes home less than her gross wage once income tax has been deducted. Define disposable income, the channel through which income tax affects households.
items.canonical_answer: Disposable income is the income households have left to spend or save after tax and other compulsory deductions have been taken from their gross income; an income tax lowers it directly, which is why its impact on households runs through their spending.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: income left after deductions, with income tax's impact running through it.
The meaning must show the channel: a tax that lowers disposable income lowers what households can spend and save.

items.prompt: Income tax rates rise across Oshakati, and 8 000 nurses, teachers and lodge workers each keep less of their pay each month. Analyse the consequences for these households, the shops they buy from and the treasury.
items.canonical_answer: A higher income tax rate lowers each worker's disposable income, the pay left after deductions. Because household spending tends to follow disposable income, the 8 000 households spend less in Oshakati's shops, transport and services, and where the rise is steep some workers may cut overtime or move into untaxed work. Therefore the households buy and save less; the shops see fewer sales and may cut staff hours, spreading the effect to other workers; and the treasury may collect less than forecast if spending weakens and taxed work shrinks.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the higher rate cutting disposable income for 8 000 workers - must be named first.
Mechanism: because spending follows disposable income, this causes fewer sales through the town's shops; the chain must be traced.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the households, the shops, the treasury - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the worker, the shopkeeper, the treasury.

items.prompt: Fuel duty of N$3 a litre is added at Swakopmund's pumps, and a tour operator there fills a 50-litre tank each working day, 22 days a month. Explain, using these figures, the impact of the duty on the operator and the passengers.
items.canonical_answer: The duty adds N$150 to each tank, since 3 x 50 = 150, and N$3 300 a month, since 150 x 22 = 3 300. Because fuel is a cost of every tour, the operator must raise fares, trim trips or accept a smaller margin. Passengers pay more for the same journey, so some take fewer trips; where competition holds fares down, the operator's margin bears more of the duty. Therefore the duty raises the operator's costs, the passengers' fares or both, while the treasury collects the N$3 300.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: N$150 a tank and about N$3 300 a month - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the duty is a cost of every journey, the link runs to fares, to trips trimmed and to the operator's margin.
Conclusion: therefore the impact lands on the operator's costs, the passengers' fares and the quantity of journeys.

items.prompt: Each year the finance ministry sets the coming year's spending plans and tax changes together in one statement. Define fiscal policy.
items.canonical_answer: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy; the yearly budget is the instrument through which the fiscal stance is set.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: spending, taxation and borrowing used to influence the economy.
The meaning must name the three parts together; a definition resting on spending alone leaves the policy half-defined.

items.prompt: A new government's first budget raises the school building programme, lifts the tax-free allowance, and plans to borrow N$8 billion across the year. Identify the features that make these measures fiscal policy.
items.canonical_answer: The features are a change in government spending (the larger school building programme), a change in taxation (the higher tax-free allowance) and a change in borrowing (N$8 billion planned). Together they move the budget's three levers, which makes them fiscal policy.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - the spending change, the tax change and the borrowing plan - as the three levers of the budget.
What it includes must be features of the stance itself; listing the policies without the levers they move earns little.

items.prompt: With work scarce in the northern regions, one budget raises public works spending and cuts the duty on building materials; with prices climbing in the south, another budget freezes the public wage bill and raises a duty. Define expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy, using these two budgets.
items.canonical_answer: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government spending or cuts taxes to lift total spending, as in the northern budget's public works and duty cut. Contractionary fiscal policy cuts spending or raises taxes to slow total spending, as in the southern budget's wage freeze and duty rise.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: expansionary measures raise spending or cut taxes to lift total spending in the economy; contractionary ones cut or raise to slow it.
The meaning must tie each measure to the direction of the stance it serves; a definition that names one lever alone - spending, taxation or borrowing - leaves the measure half-defined.

items.prompt: With workshops idle across Otavi and unemployment high, the budget raises public spending on the town's water scheme by N$40 million a year and borrows the sum rather than raising taxes. Analyse how these measures work through Otavi's economy and its future budgets.
items.canonical_answer: N$40 million a year of new borrowed spending arrives where workshops are idle and unemployment is high, so there is spare capacity. Because contractors give the work to local firms and hire idle workers, incomes rise and circulate through Otavi's shops and suppliers, and with spare capacity the extra spending tends to raise output and jobs rather than prices. Therefore the builders gain work, their households gain wages, the shops gain takings and the treasury gains tax revenue; but future budgets carry the borrowing, whose interest and repayments fall on later taxpayers.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - N$40 million of borrowed spending arriving where workshops are idle - must be named first.
Mechanism: because the spending reaches an economy with spare capacity, this causes output and employment to rise rather than prices.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the builders, the shops, the future budgets - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the worker, the shopkeeper, the later taxpayer.

items.prompt: Prices in Windhoek have climbed for six months running, and the budget answers by freezing the public wage bill and raising the duty on new vehicles. Explain, from these measures, how a contractionary fiscal stance is meant to slow the climb.
items.canonical_answer: The budget takes spending power out of the economy: public workers' pay is frozen and the duty makes new vehicles dearer, after six months of rising prices. Because households and firms have less to spend, buying cools, and firms facing weaker demand tend to hold prices to win sales rather than raise them. Therefore the stance slows the price climb, though it squeezes public workers' living costs, and where rising costs such as fuel or imports drive prices, it may slow the climb rather than stop it.
marking_guidance: The context - the extract: the frozen wage bill and the dearer duty against six months of climbing prices - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the measures trim spending power, the link runs to weaker buying and firms holding prices for custom.
Conclusion: therefore the stance leans on the climb through spending, with its limits - the workers' living costs and cost-push pressures - named.

items.prompt: With work scarce in the northern regions, the new budget raises public works spending, aiming to bring unemployment down. Define an expansionary fiscal measure and its intended effect on a macroeconomic aim.
items.canonical_answer: An expansionary fiscal measure raises government spending or cuts taxes to lift total spending in the economy, here the extra public works. Its intended effect is lower unemployment: where there is spare capacity, the works raise output and employment rather than prices.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a measure that raises government spending or cuts taxes to lift total spending in the economy, tied to the aim it targets.

The meaning must carry the effect with its condition - where there is spare capacity the spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices - since the aim is reached under that condition.

items.prompt: The standard rate of income tax is cut, households across Windhoek keep more of each pay packet, and workshops in the industrial areas sit part-empty. Analyse the effects of the cut on the macroeconomic aims of employment, growth and price stability.
items.canonical_answer: The income tax cut raises households' disposable income across Windhoek. Because spending tends to follow disposable income, buying in shops and services rises, and with the workshops part-empty there is spare capacity, so firms hire to raise output: the employment and growth aims gain. The government loses revenue and must borrow more or spend less elsewhere. As capacity fills, the same extra spending tends to push prices up, so the price-stability aim turns against the jobs. Therefore workers gain jobs and firms gain sales, while savers and fixed-income households lose if prices rise, and the government's budget carries the shortfall.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the lower rate lifting disposable income where workshops sit part-empty - must be named first.
Mechanism: because spending follows disposable income and capacity is spare, this causes output and employment to rise before prices.
Consequence: therefore each named aim - employment, growth, price stability - needs its own traced outcome, including the aims turning against one another.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the worker, the firm, the saver on a fixed income, the government's budget.

items.prompt: A government has raised its spending on clinics for five years, paying for it by borrowing. In one region 6 000 young people are out of work, and prices across the country have begun to rise faster. Explain, from these facts, how fiscal policy can move two macroeconomic aims against one another.
items.canonical_answer: The data show expansionary fiscal policy: five years of rising clinic spending funded by borrowing, with 6 000 young people still out of work and prices starting to rise faster. Where spare capacity remains, more government spending tends to raise output and create jobs, serving the employment aim. As capacity fills, the extra spending tends to push prices up, straining the low-inflation aim. Cutting spending to slow prices would cost the young jobs. Therefore the employment and low-inflation aims pull against one another.
marking_guidance: Context: the data - five years of borrowed clinic spending, 6 000 young people out of work, prices beginning to rise faster - must anchor the answer.

Reasoning: because spending supports jobs while spare capacity remains and pushes prices up as capacity fills, the link is one stance moving the employment and inflation aims in opposite directions; health care is a reason for spending, not a macroeconomic aim.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must state that the employment and low-inflation aims pull against one another.

items.prompt: Define a budget deficit.
items.canonical_answer: A budget deficit is the amount by which a government's spending exceeds its revenue over a period, usually a year. The gap tends to be covered by borrowing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: one mark for government spending exceeding government revenue, and one for the period (usually a year) or for the gap being covered by borrowing. A definition comparing exports with imports describes a current account deficit, a different balance, and earns nothing.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define a budget surplus.
items.canonical_answer: A budget surplus is the amount by which a government's revenue exceeds its spending over a period, usually a year. The surplus can be used to repay past borrowing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: one mark for government revenue exceeding government spending, and one for the period (usually a year) or for the use of the surplus to repay past borrowing. Revenue and spending must both be the government's; a surplus of exports over imports is a different balance.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: In one year a government collects N$58 billion in taxes and N$4 billion from fees and other sources, and spends N$67 billion. Calculate the size of its budget deficit or surplus.
items.canonical_answer: Budget balance = total revenue - total spending. Revenue: 58 + 4 = 62, so N$62 billion. Balance: 62 - 67 = -5, a budget deficit of N$5 billion.
marking_guidance: Formula: budget balance = total government revenue - total government spending must be stated or used.
Substitution: the working adds the N$58 billion and N$4 billion of revenue before subtracting the N$67 billion of spending.
Answer with units: a budget deficit of N$5 billion - the word deficit or the minus sign must be given, with N$ billion.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A government's budget is balanced, with N$70 billion of revenue and N$70 billion of spending. The new budget raises spending on school building by N$3 billion and cuts income tax rates, which is expected to lower revenue by N$2 billion. Explain how these fiscal measures change the budget balance.
items.canonical_answer: Both measures widen the gap between spending and revenue. Spending rises to N$73 billion, since 70 + 3 = 73, and revenue falls to N$68 billion, since 70 - 2 = 68. Because spending now exceeds revenue, the balanced budget becomes a deficit of N$5 billion, since 73 - 68 = 5, which tends to be borrowed. Where the tax cut raises spending and incomes, some revenue may return through sales and income taxes, so the deficit may turn out smaller than N$5 billion.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - the N$70 billion balanced budget, the N$3 billion spending rise and the N$2 billion fall in revenue.
Reasoning: the link must be given - because a spending rise and a tax cut each push spending above revenue, the balance moves from balanced to deficit.
Conclusion: therefore the budget moves to a deficit of N$5 billion, possibly smaller where higher incomes return some tax revenue.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why taxation is the main source of government revenue.
items.canonical_answer: A tax is compulsory and falls on the incomes, spending and profits of the whole economy, so even modest rates applied to so large a base raise large sums every year. The other sources are smaller or less reliable: fees cover particular services, profits of state-owned enterprises rise and fall with their trading, selling a state asset raises money once, and foreign grants vary from year to year. Borrowing is not revenue at all, because it must be repaid with interest.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose must be stated - taxation raises the largest sums - because it is compulsory and its base is the income, spending and profit of the whole economy.

Development: credit each other source set against it - fees, profits of state-owned enterprises, asset sales, foreign grants - with the reason each is smaller or less reliable, and the point that borrowing is a debt, not revenue.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define a proportional tax.
items.canonical_answer: A proportional tax takes the same percentage of income whatever the size of the income. The amount paid rises with income but the share does not: a flat 20% tax takes N$2 000 from N$10 000 and N$6 000 from N$30 000.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: one mark for the same percentage (share) of income at every level of income, and one for the boundary - the amount paid may rise with income while the share stays fixed. Calling a tax progressive because richer people pay more money confuses the amount with the share.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Identify two qualities of a good tax other than equity, certainty, convenience and economy.
items.canonical_answer: Any two of: efficiency - it raises revenue without strongly discouraging work, saving or investment; flexibility - its rate can be changed easily as the economy's needs change; difficulty of evasion - it is hard to dodge, as with income tax deducted from wages.
marking_guidance: Features: one mark for each quality identified, up to two - efficiency (little disincentive to work, save or invest), flexibility, or difficulty of evasion. Equity, certainty, convenience or economy earn nothing, because the prompt excludes them.

items.prompt: A government raises the rate of company tax on firms' profits from 28% to 34%, while neighbouring countries keep their rates near 28%. Analyse the possible effects of this tax rise on the economy as a whole.
items.canonical_answer: The rise takes N$6 more of every N$100 of profit, so firms keep less to reinvest. Because profit after tax falls, firms tend to cut investment, and foreign firms deciding where to build may choose neighbouring countries where about 28% still applies. This causes fewer new factories and jobs, so growth and employment tend to slow, and some firms may pass part of the tax on in higher prices. The government gains revenue at first, but if investment moves abroad the tax base shrinks and later revenue may fall short. Therefore workers may face fewer new jobs, consumers higher prices, and the government a gain that may not last.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - company tax rising from 28% to 34% while neighbours stay near 28% - must be named first.
Mechanism: because firms keep less profit after tax, this causes investment to fall or move to lower-tax neighbours.
Consequence: therefore growth, employment, prices and later tax revenue each need a traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - workers, consumers, firms and the government.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Namibia imports most of its vehicles, fuel and machinery. Suppose its current account deficit has widened, and the government raises income tax rates and cuts some of its own spending. Explain how these fiscal measures may affect the current account deficit.
items.canonical_answer: Higher income tax and lower government spending leave households and firms with less to spend. Because a large part of Namibian spending goes on imported vehicles, fuel and machinery, spending on imports tends to fall, so payments abroad fall and the current account deficit tends to narrow. The cost lands at home: local firms also sell less, so growth slows and jobs may be lost. Therefore the measures may reduce the current account deficit, but at the expense of the growth and employment aims.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the high share of imports in Namibian spending and the two measures - higher income tax and lower government spending.
Reasoning: the link must be given - because disposable income and spending fall, spending on imports falls, so payments abroad fall.
Conclusion: therefore the current account deficit tends to narrow, at the cost of slower growth and fewer jobs.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A government raises the income tax rate paid on the highest incomes and uses the extra revenue to increase grants paid to low-income households. Analyse the effects of these measures on the distribution of income.
items.canonical_answer: The higher top rate takes a larger share of high incomes, so incomes after tax at the top fall. Because the revenue funds larger grants, spending power is transferred to low-income households, whose incomes rise. This causes the gap between high and low incomes after tax to narrow, so more poor households can afford food, schooling and clinic visits. However, if high earners respond by working less, investing less or moving income abroad, the revenue raised falls short and the grants may be smaller than planned. Therefore low-income households gain, high earners lose, and how far the gap narrows depends on how strongly high earners react.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - a higher tax rate on the highest incomes, with the revenue spent on grants to low-income households - must be named first.
Mechanism: because income is taken from the top and transferred to the bottom, this causes incomes after tax to move closer together.
Consequence: therefore the income gap narrows, by less where high earners work, invest or declare less.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - low-income households, high earners and the government's revenue.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. The government budget is best defined as:
A  the record of last year's tax receipts
B  the yearly plan of expected revenue and intended spending
C  the stock of money the government holds
D  the law that sets up the revenue authority

2. A country's imports of goods and services exceed its exports, while its government's revenue exceeds its spending. The country has:
A  a budget deficit and a current account surplus
B  a budget surplus and a current account deficit
C  both a budget deficit and a current account deficit
D  a balanced budget and a current account surplus

3. A tax is:
A  a payment for a service received from the state
B  a compulsory levy on income, spending or wealth
C  a penalty imposed on law-breakers
D  a loan the government repays with interest

4. Which is an indirect tax?
A  income tax on a nurse's wage
B  company tax on a firm's profit
C  value-added tax added to a shop bill
D  a weekly levy on each worker's wage

5. An income tax is progressive where:
A  everyone pays the same amount
B  the share of income taken rises as income rises
C  the share of income taken falls as income rises
D  the rate is the same whatever the payer earns

6. After a fuel duty rise, a haulier cut two routes. Which states the direction correctly?
A  the duty rise caused the route cuts
B  the route cuts caused the duty rise
C  the two events are unrelated
D  the duty rise and the cuts are the same event

7. Which is a fiscal policy measure?
A  raising the interest rate banks charge
B  raising the standard rate of income tax
C  lowering the price of foreign currency
D  licensing a second mobile operator

8. Fiscal policy is the use of:
A  interest rates and lending rules
B  government spending, taxation and borrowing
C  laws to control dominant sellers
D  duties charged on imported goods alone
items.canonical_answer:
1 B. The budget is a plan for the year ahead pairing revenue with spending. A catches the learner who treats the budget as a record of the past rather than a plan; C catches the confusion of the budget with the government's cash; D catches the confusion of the budget with the law that creates the tax office.
2 B. Revenue above spending is a budget surplus; imports above exports is a current account deficit. A and C catch the budget-deficit-versus-current-account-deficit confusion, treating the two balances as one; D catches the learner who reads one surplus as both.
3 B. A tax is compulsory and owed regardless of service. A catches the learner who treats a tax as a price; C catches the confusion of taxes with penalties; D catches the confusion of taxes with borrowing.
4 C. Value-added tax is levied on spending and collected by the seller. A and B catch the learner who classifies the income and profit charges as indirect; D catches the boundary drawn the wrong way round - a levy on a wage, handed over from it, is direct.
5 B. Progression turns on the share of income rising with income. A catches the confusion of progressive with a flat amount; C states the regressive case; D catches the confusion of progressive with proportional in rate terms.
6 A. The tax change is the cause and the route cuts are its consequence. B catches a common error - writing the consequences of a tax increase as its cause; C and D catch accounts that abandon the direction of events altogether.
7 B. A tax change is the budget's own lever. A catches the learner who reaches for the interest rate - the price of borrowing - which is monetary policy's lever, not fiscal policy's; C catches the exchange-rate confusion; D catches the confusion of fiscal policy with regulation.
8 B. The three levers are spending, taxation and borrowing. A catches the interest-rate confusion again; C catches the confusion with competition policy; D narrows fiscal policy to one narrow duty and catches the learner who forgets the spending and borrowing levers.
marking_guidance: One mark per question; the key and the distractor explanations are the teaching back of the set.

Each distractor explanation names the specific misunderstanding it catches - the direct-versus-indirect boundary, the consequence-versus-cause direction, the interest-rate-versus-tax confusion, and the budget-versus-current-account balances.
Questions 2, 4 and 6 carry the topic's registered misconceptions, so their distractor explanations are the discrimination itself.

items.prompt:
A radio report from Oshakati, May 2027: "The town council is weighing a N$2 a litre levy on sugary drinks sold through the town's 40 licensed outlets. The state clinic's wards treated 3 000 sugar-related cases last year, and the council met N$4.5 million of their cost. Outlets sold 300 000 litres last year at prices the levy would raise."

Table 1 - the levy, as proposed
  rate: N$2 a litre
  litres sold last year: 300 000
  clinic cost met by the council: N$4.5 million
  outlets covered: 40

(a) Calculate the revenue the levy would have raised on last year's sales. [1]
(b) Identify from the report one feature that makes the levy an indirect tax, and one reason the council is weighing it. [2]
(c) Explain why the levy's burden may weigh more heavily on poorer households in Oshakati. [4]
(d) Analyse what the levy would do to the town's drinking, its outlets and the clinic, using the data as evidence. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 300 000 x 2 = 600 000; the levy would have raised N$600 000 on last year's litres.
(b) The levy is added to the price of each litre and collected by the outlet from the buyer - a tax on spending collected by traders, which is what makes it indirect. The council is weighing it to make the price carry more of the N$4.5 million of clinic cost that drinking imposes on others, and to discourage the drinking that fills the wards.
(c) A poorer household spends a larger part of its income on drinks and food generally, so the same N$2 a litre takes a larger share of a poor household's income than of a rich one's - the levy is regressive in effect. Because poorer households also tend to buy the sugary drinks most heavily, they bear more of the charge; and where they keep buying out of habit, they are less able than richer households to switch to untaxed choices.
(d) The levy raises the price, so the quantity of sugary drinks demanded tends to fall, easing the harm the wards pay for. The data support this: 300 000 litres sold against a N$4.5 million clinic bill, with the N$2 rate raising N$600 000 towards that bill if sales held. For the outlets, fewer litres spread across 40 counters trims takings and may cut staff hours; for the drinkers, the price rise deters light buyers first, while the heaviest keep buying and bear the regressive weight; for the clinic, fewer sugar-related cases ease the N$4.5 million burden, and the levy's revenue can fund the wards directly. The exception is where habit keeps demand strong: litres may then fall very little, the wards see little relief, and the levy works mainly as a revenue raiser on poorer households' spending.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the 300 000 litres, the N$2 rate, the N$4.5 million - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c) and (d): a relationship, a reason or a named consequence counts where it is linked, not merely listed.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for the outlets, the drinkers and the clinic, each with its own traced outcome.

items.prompt:
Answer all parts.

(a) Define fiscal policy. [2]
(b) Explain two reasons why the government, rather than private firms, funds the Otavi water scheme and the clinics that serve it. [4]
(c) The budget raises public spending on a new district training college by N$40 million a year, funded by borrowing, with 300 builders idle in the district and construction firms working below capacity. Analyse the effects of this measure on the macroeconomic aims of employment, growth and price stability. [6]
(d) Discuss whether the government should cut income taxes rather than raise spending when unemployment is high but prices are climbing. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy, with the yearly budget as its instrument.
(b) The water scheme is close to a public good: clean water for the town's households cannot sensibly be confined to those who pay, so a private firm would tend to provide too little of it - the government funds it because the market left alone would under-provide. The clinics are merit goods: households undervalue check-ups and treatment until illness makes them urgent, so left to pay directly they would consume less than the district's health requires; public funding corrects that under-consumption. The two reasons - the under-provided public good and the under-consumed merit good - are the standard cases for public spending.
(c) N$40 million a year of borrowed public spending on the college arrives in a district with 300 builders idle and firms working below capacity, so there is clear spare capacity. Because the building work hires the idle builders and sends orders to construction firms, incomes rise and circulate through the district's suppliers and shops; with capacity spare, the extra spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices. Therefore the growth aim gains as output rises, the employment aim gains as the builders and further workers are drawn in, and the price-stability aim holds while capacity is spare. As capacity tightens, later spending tends to push prices up, and the borrowing weighs on future budgets, whose repayments fall on later taxpayers. The builders and firms gain now, the district's shops gain through the wage chain, and later taxpayers meet the repayments.
(d) A tax cut answers high unemployment quickly: it lifts disposable income at once, and where there is spare capacity the extra spending tends to raise output and jobs rather than prices, with the payroll already in place to deliver it. Against it, with prices climbing already, the same extra spending tends to add pressure to prices as capacity tightens, so the cut risks moving one aim against another; a cut in the standard rate gives more to higher earners, so its reach is regressive; and the revenue it surrenders widens the budget gap, shifting repayment onto later budgets. On balance, where unemployment is the sharper problem and capacity is plainly spare, the cut is justified; the judgement depends on how close the economy is to full capacity - the closer it is, the stronger the case for targeted spending or for holding the stance.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: spending, taxation and borrowing used to influence the economy.
(b) one mark per distinct reason with its link made: the public-good case and the merit-good case, each carried to its consequence.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - N$40 million arriving where 300 builders are idle - through the mechanism to the consequence for each named aim; the spare-capacity condition earns its place.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - spending power and jobs where capacity is spare - and why it might not - pressure on prices, regressive reach, the wider gap - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The budget deficit stands at N$8 billion in a year when workshops sit idle. Discuss whether the government should borrow less." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for borrowing less: the deficit shifts today's spending onto future taxpayers, who meet the interest from later budgets. Chain 1: borrowing falls -> the debt and its interest bill grow more slowly -> later budgets spend less on interest, leaving more for schools and clinics or room for lower taxes -> future taxpayers and service users gain (for the later taxpayer, the service user).
Case against borrowing less - for holding or raising it: with capacity spare, public spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices, and cutting borrowing now would trim programmes or raise taxes while workshops sit idle, so output and jobs would tend to fall further. Chain 2: borrowed funds build the water scheme or the college -> the idle workshops are hired -> household incomes rise and the tax base widens -> later repayments are met from a larger output (for the worker, the firm, the later taxpayer).
Judgement: the case for borrowing turns on the condition - where the funds buy capacity-raising projects and the economy has spare capacity, the N$8 billion is justified; where they fund current consumption near full capacity, borrowing less is the better course.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from the measure to its consequence, and name the parties - the worker, the taxpayer, the later taxpayer.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: what the borrowed funds buy, and how much capacity is spare.
What settles it: whether the borrowing raises the economy's productive capacity against merely funding the present - the decisive test is what the funds buy and the state of capacity.
